papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Pre-training Plus Strategic Distillation: Practical Principles for Compressing Deep NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are most effective when combined with deliberate choices about pre-training, the form of knowledge transferred, data manipulation during distillation, and adaptive teacher-student dynamics. Compact models that are pre-trained, trained to mimic both outputs and internal representations, and exposed to carefully designed augmented or mixed inputs can match much of the performance of larger models while meeting deployment constraints. However, compression success depends critically on optimization, data distribution, and task-specific phenomena such as rare-word behavior in sequence generation. I argue that a pragmatic pipeline—pre-train compact architectures, distill soft targets and internal representations, use augmentation/mixing to shape training data complexity, and apply adaptive or meta-learned teacher strategies—offers the best trade-off between efficiency and accuracy for deep learning and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision models while retaining much of their performance. Approaches range from matching teacher soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations and using contrastive or projection-based objectives. Practical training choices—such as which layers or features to mimic, how to filter or weight training samples, the role of data augmentation, and whether compact models are pre-trained—strongly affect outcomes. KD has been applied across domains (vision, language, graphs), combined with quantization and low-precision deployment, and adapted for resource-heterogeneous and latency-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights that KD works both by transferring relational/representational knowledge and by providing regularizing soft targets; effective distillation designs balance these mechanisms and tailor the transfer to task and capacity constraints.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster models while preserving— and in some settings improving—accuracy, robustness, and domain suitability. KD can be adapted to resource-constrained deployment, domain adaptation, privacy- or data-limited settings, and to improve adversarial robustness when paired with targeted techniques. Combining KD with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning, structured sparsity, layer mapping) yields practical, high-quality compressed models across modalities including vision, language, graphs, and generative models.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Practical Advances
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations. Research has developed many variants — logits-based soft-labels, feature- and attention-based matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, self-distillation, and data-free approaches — and applied them across vision, language, recommendation, and healthcare. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the practical benefits (faster inference, lower memory, domain adaptation, interpretability) and core limitations (optimization obstacles, capacity mismatch, distributional effects), motivating techniques that alter what is distilled, how it is matched, and even how teachers are trained to be more amenable to students.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). In practice KD has been applied to compress large pre-trained language models, enable fast inference in NLP, adapt models to new domains or tasks, support heterogeneous and federated settings, and enable data-free scenarios. Approaches differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single vs multi-teacher, jointly trained teachers), and how training data is used or synthesized. Empirical results show KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of task performance, but success depends on choices around layer mapping, feature vs. logit supervision, data complexity, and training protocols. Open challenges include handling data heterogeneity, optimizing teacher-student pairings, and ensuring stable distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central strategy for compressing large neural networks into compact, deployable models across computer vision, generative modeling, and natural language processing. KD techniques extend beyond matching teacher output probabilities to include distillation of intermediate representations, layer-level mappings, and training without access to original data. Practical applications span compressing generative adversarial networks, pre-trained language models, and low-precision networks, while also addressing robustness and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation protocols can retain most of a teacher's performance or even improve downstream robustness and inference efficiency, though success depends on choices such as what knowledge to transfer, architectural alignment, and availability of data or suitable synthetic surrogates.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Settings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models or ensembles to smaller “student” models. Work in this area spans methods that match final outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure; approaches that adapt teacher signals through meta-learning or task-aware filters; and specializations for settings such as vision–language, graph learning, federated or distributed training, and data-free scenarios. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but practical success depends on handling domain shift, architectural mismatch, heterogeneous data and devices, and the quality or calibration of teacher outputs. Important theoretical and statistical analyses have begun to clarify when and why distillation helps, but open problems remain around robust, privacy-preserving, and architecture-agnostic distillation for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used technique to transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. It serves both model compression and training-stabilization roles across vision, speech, and language tasks. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online/co-distillation among peers, feature- and representation-level matching, and hybrid schemes that combine distillation with quantization or specialized training objectives. Empirical evidence shows KD can improve accuracy, generalization, robustness, and inference efficiency, but its success depends on data complexity, teacher design, and the type of knowledge transferred.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones across modalities (classification, sequence modeling, generation, graph-structured data, and federated systems). KD’s strengths arise not only from transferring teacher logits but also from transferring richer representation-level, adversarial, and self-derived signals. However, distillation has well-documented failure modes—optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, and domain or device heterogeneity—that require specific remedies. Combining representation-level objectives, teacher-friendly training, self-distillation or teacher-free approaches, and careful data strategies yields more robust and efficient compressed models while avoiding common pitfalls.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role and Evolving Practices of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a fundamental and versatile approach for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning and NLP. It enables compact, efficient student models that retain much of a teacher's performance, supports deployment on resource-constrained devices, and can be adapted to privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. Recent advances extend distillation beyond simple logits matching to many-to-many layer mapping, task-adaptive compression, teacher-aware training, adversarial and data-free scenarios, and robustness-aware objectives. Together these developments show that distillation is both a practical engineering tool and a rich research paradigm for addressing capacity, data availability, privacy, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a flexible paradigm that improves efficiency, robustness, privacy, and generalization across modalities and tasks. KD can compress large pretrained models into lightweight deployable models, transfer internal representations to preserve teacher behaviors, operate without original training data, and be adapted to distributed and privacy-sensitive settings. Recent methodological advances—layer- and attention-aware projection, multi-teacher schedules, meta-learned teachers, and techniques connecting KD to regularization—make distillation a practical and theoretically grounded tool for both research and production NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured beyond a single recipe for copying soft labels: it is a flexible set of techniques that address model compression, domain and task transfer, privacy-constrained scenarios, distributed training, and continual learning. Practical KD variants operate at different levels (logits, features, layers), use data augmentation or synthetic data when real data are unavailable, and adapt training schedules to the target application. When chosen to match the constraints of the deployment setting—data availability, compute budget, task type, and model architecture—KD consistently enables smaller or more specialized students to approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance while offering operational benefits such as faster inference, lower memory, and more reproducible training.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, machine translation, reading comprehension, and large-scale distributed training—recent work shows KD can improve inference speed, aid domain adaptation, enable training without original data, and increase robustness. Combining innovations in layer mapping, feature-level transfer, online and data-free techniques, and teacher optimization yields the best trade-offs for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of practical and theoretical approaches for shrinking deep models while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, layer- and feature-level matching, architecture-aware transformations, teacher improvement or selection strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving pipelines, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-transfer applications, recent work shows that careful design choices—such as how layers are matched, which features to transfer, whether the teacher is static or trained to teach, and how to handle limited or private data—substantially affect the student’s final accuracy and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical and Multifaceted Engine for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical set of techniques that enable deploying high-performing deep models under computation, memory, data, and privacy constraints. By transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure from large teachers to compact students, KD supports domain specialization, model acceleration, privacy-preserving release, and improved generalization. Best results come from matching the KD strategy to the constraints and goals of the application (e.g., multi-teacher aggregation, representation-level transfer, data-free generation, or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: The Case for Practical, Adaptive Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible tool for compressing large deep learning models into deployable students. Recent work shows KD can both directly reduce model size and serve as a mechanism to transfer inductive biases, intermediate representations, and task-specific attention. However, real-world constraints — limited or private training data, domain and client heterogeneity, and redundant teacher representations — require KD methods that are data-free, adversarially robust, task-aware, and selective about what teacher knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable transfer of predictive power from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The literature has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include internal-representation distillation, module replacement, self-distillation, selective sample transfer, and adaptations for constraints such as privacy, communication, and low-precision inference. Applied across domains—from NLP rankers and translation to graph, vision-language, and speech systems—these methods trade off fidelity, efficiency, and robustness through a variety of algorithmic and engineering solutions.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been widely adopted to reduce model size and runtime while retaining performance. Work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows multiple complementary strategies—logit matching, feature mimicking, layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, and self-distillation—can be effective alone or in combination. Practical success depends on choices about teacher strength, student architecture, pre-training, and optimization, and recent systems integrate distillation with pruning, low-precision, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods have become central tools for deploying large deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. Work in this area spans techniques that transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller students, approaches that operate without access to original training data, methods that preserve privacy or reduce communication in distributed settings, and specialized strategies for large pre-trained language and vision transformer models. Key themes include layer- and module-level mappings between teacher and student, task-aware selection of distilled signals, adversarial and generative approaches to synthesize training inputs, and the combination of pruning or architecture search with distillation. Practical trade-offs arise between fidelity to teacher behavior, student capacity, data availability, and robustness to distribution shifts or adversarial attacks. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous modalities and architectures, selecting what information to transfer for a given downstream task, and ensuring privacy and robustness while maintaining high compression ratios.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment. A diverse set of strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and intermediate representation matching to multi-teacher ensembles, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-supervised or privacy-preserving protocols—have been developed to preserve accuracy, robustness, and modality transfer while reducing inference cost. Practical systems combine distillation with quantization, pruning, or architecture search to meet application-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to obtain compact models that retain much of the performance of larger models. Beyond simple logits matching, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, task-adaptive compression, privacy-preserving model release, and synergizes with structural compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints in real-world systems. This article argues that KD should be a central component of modern model-compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, both in practice and in research directions.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and allied compression techniques have become central tools for reducing the computational and storage cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original soft-label paradigm to include distillation of internal representations, layer- and channel-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, and teacher-student co-design. Applications span vision, NLP, graph models, generative networks, and large-scale distributed training. Recent work also explores distillation for robustness, low-precision deployment, few-shot compression, and federated or multi-device settings. Despite strong empirical gains, open challenges remain in transferring inductive biases, choosing what and when to distill, and preserving attributes such as fairness and adversarial robustness in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, multi-faceted approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Beyond simple teacher-student logits matching, distillation can be adapted to transfer inductive biases, deploy in federated or privacy-constrained settings, operate without access to original training data, and improve robustness and domain specialization. When combined with techniques such as feature mimicking, careful soft-label regularization, and online or ensemble-based training regimes, distillation provides a flexible toolkit to meet the efficiency, privacy, and deployment constraints of modern deep learning and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavioral or representational information from a teacher to a student. Across computer vision and NLP, distillation methods vary from matching output soft targets to aligning internal representations, performing self-distillation, and synthesizing or selecting data when original training examples are unavailable. Empirical work shows distillation can retain much of teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, improved generalization, and deployment under latency or memory constraints. However, effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, layers, features), the availability and complexity of training data, regularization (e.g., label smoothing and augmentation), and fairness or privacy constraints. Open challenges include understanding when students can outperform teachers, balancing bias mitigation and utility, and combining distillation with pruning or hardware-aware compression for edge deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Methods, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or costly models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Research over the past decade shows multiple complementary mechanisms for effective distillation—soft-target supervision, feature and representation mimicking, layer-wise alignment, and task-aware selection of teacher knowledge. Practical advances adapt distillation to domain constraints (few-shot data, modality mismatch, federated or latency-constrained deployment) and model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph neural networks, generative models). Empirical work demonstrates that thoughtful choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features vs. relations), how to align layers, and how to prepare data and pretraining substantially affect student performance, sometimes enabling students to match or even surpass teachers under resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Methods, Limits, and Complementary Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy to compress large pre-trained deep models so they can be deployed in latency- and resource-constrained settings. KD variants—multi-teacher pipelines, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, self-distillation, and feature-level matching—enable small students to approach or match teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost. KD is most effective when combined with complementary approaches such as pruning and architecture search, and when adapted to domain or system constraints (e.g., federated or multi-device settings). However, KD is not a universal panacea: data heterogeneity, misaligned inputs between teacher and student, and inappropriate augmentation or feature transfer can limit gains, so careful design choices are required to realize practical compression.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original logit-based teacher-student paradigm to include feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher strategies, and task- or hardware-aware compression. These methods have been applied across modalities — including vision, graphs, generative models, and a broad set of NLP tasks — and are increasingly combined with architecture search and pruning to meet deployment constraints. Despite empirical successes, important questions remain about what knowledge is most useful to transfer, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to operate under data, compute, or privacy limitations.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient ones while preserving accuracy. Beyond raw model size reduction, KD enables applications that require interpretable models, heterogeneous and privacy-preserving deployments, and multi-task or low-resource inference. However, distillation is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher biases (especially on rare tokens or classes) and can be sensitive to data availability and heterogeneity. Best practice therefore combines KD with careful sample selection, architectural mediators for feature transfer, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, or generator-based data synthesis) to achieve robust, deployable student models.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

Work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows multiple complementary strategies—logit matching, feature mimicking, layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, and self-distillation—can be effective alone or in combination. Practical success depends on choices about teacher strength, student architecture, pre-training, and optimization, and recent systems integrate distillation with pruning, low-precision, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints.'}, {'author': 'Cannon', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods have become central tools for deploying large deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. Practical trade-offs arise between fidelity to teacher behavior, student capacity, data availability, and robustness to distribution shifts or adversarial attacks. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous modalities and architectures, selecting what information to transfer for a given downstream task, and ensuring privacy and robustness while maintaining high compression ratios.'}, {'author': 'Reid', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions', 'abstract': 'Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.'}, {'author': 'Parsons', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation', 'abstract': "Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework."}, {'author': 'Daniels', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment.
