papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Pathways for Compressing Large NLP Models: Pre-train the Student, Distill Carefully, and Guard for Data & Robustness
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach to compress large deep learning models for NLP and related tasks. When the student model is itself pre-trained, distillation yields especially strong and consistent gains; complementary methods — including data augmentation during distillation, progressive module replacement, ensemble teachers or teacher adaptation, and data-free or privacy-aware distillation — address common deployment constraints such as limited task data, inference cost, data access, and adversarial robustness. Combining these techniques and choosing distillation targets and schedules with theoretical and empirical guidance yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool to make large deep models practical: it reduces model size and latency, enables domain adaptation, preserves privacy and scalability, and can even improve robustness when applied carefully. Successful deployments balance which teacher signals are transferred (logits, features, attention or answers), how they are aligned (layer-wise, projector-mediated, task-aware filters), and the training setup (multi-teacher, online, or adversarial). I argue that a principled combination of feature-level guidance, task-aware selection, and appropriate distillation architecture gives the best tradeoffs for NLP deployment: it preserves downstream performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude gains in speed, capacity, and deployability.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable tool for reducing model size and inference cost while preserving (or even improving) performance. Beyond straightforward teacher→student logit matching, KD can be applied structurally (transforming architectures without redesign), combined with quantization, used for domain adaptation of large pretrained language models, leveraged in multi-teacher and few-shot settings, and operated without access to original data. KD’s benefits arise both from transferring predictive behavior and from inducing effective regularization; when paired with careful choices (e.g., feature projectors, divergence measures, or pseudo-replay for data-free settings), KD enables deployment of compact, reliable models across vision, speech, language, graph, and generative-model domains.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation unifies multiple strategies for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable models while preserving performance. It supports a range of goals — parameter and latency reduction, robustness, interpretability, and privacy-aware deployment — by transferring information from a teacher to a student via soft outputs, intermediate representations, or structural/architectural guidance. Practical and research advances show that combining distillation modes (feature-level, output-level, progressive module replacement), data augmentation, and adaptive teacher training yields compact models that approach teacher performance even under limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Task-Aware, and Privacy-Conscious Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment across modalities and tasks. Effective KD goes beyond naive logits matching: task-aware layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher schedules, and architecture-aware search can preserve accuracy while reducing compute and memory. Moreover, self-distillation and teacher-free variants reduce dependence on strong teachers, and specialized KD variants address scarce data, privacy, and federated constraints. These directions together form a roadmap for applying KD in real-world deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression techniques compress or replace large pretrained models with smaller, efficient models while aiming to retain much of the original performance. Modern work spans logit-based soft-label distillation, feature- and attention-based representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, online and mutual distillation schemes, meta-learned teachers, and approaches for resource- or data-constrained scenarios (including data-free and few-shot settings). Applications include compressing large language models into lightweight architectures for deployment, accelerating visual and multimodal models, enabling distributed training, and improving robustness and transfer. Key challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align heterogeneous architectures, preventing capacity mismatch and overfitting, and preserving task-relevant information while removing redundant representations. Empirical strategies that combine representation-level losses, task-aware selection, and online or meta-learning mechanisms tend to yield the best tradeoffs between efficiency and retained accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models and transferring their capabilities to smaller or specialized models. KD can operate at multiple levels (logits, intermediate layers, and features), can be combined with model pruning and precision reduction, and can support domain adaptation and on-device deployment. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on how teacher knowledge is represented and transferred, the choice of data and augmentations used during distillation, and the deployment context (e.g., heterogeneous federated environments). When methods for intermediate-layer alignment, feature mimicking, data-side regularization, and architecture-aware mapping are combined thoughtfully, KD yields compact, efficient models that retain much of the teacher’s performance while enabling practical deployment in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, machine translation, reading comprehension, and large-scale distributed training—recent work shows KD can improve inference speed, aid domain adaptation, enable training without original data, and increase robustness. Combining innovations in layer mapping, feature-level transfer, online and data-free techniques, and teacher optimization yields the best trade-offs for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for transferring soft targets into a unifying toolkit that enables model compression, deployment on constrained devices, privacy-aware release, and modality transfer. By combining architectural mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, and data-free or federated setups, KD can preserve much of a teacher model's performance while drastically reducing footprint and computation. This makes KD essential for translating state-of-the-art large models into real-world, resource-limited, and privacy-sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Engine for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a heuristic into a set of principled, modality-agnostic techniques that enable deployment of high-capacity models in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings. By transferring predictive behaviour and internal representations from large teachers to compact students, distillation preserves much of the teacher's utility while enabling large speed, memory, and communication gains. Recent advances show that combining representation-level matching, teacher–student co-design, data-free synthesis, and task-adaptive compression yields robust, practical pipelines for compressing models across vision, language, graph, and federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and accelerates large neural models by transferring information from one or more teacher models into a smaller student. Across vision and language, KD variants extend from logit-matching to feature- and attention-level transfer, multi-teacher ensembling, online/co-distillation, privacy-aware and federated setups, and combinations with quantization or structured pruning. Practical pipelines combine KD with architecture-aware transformations, domain adaptation, and task-specific pretraining to obtain compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Despite empirical success across modalities and deployment settings, trade-offs remain in teacher selection, information type to transfer, stability for heterogeneous architectures, and theoretical interpretation of what is transferred; these motivate further research into adaptive teacher weighting, feature alignment layers, and scalable privacy-preserving distillation for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while attempting to retain performance. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD variants address constraints such as limited computation, on-device heterogeneity, lack of access to teacher training data, fairness concerns, and the need for task-specific efficiency. Common themes include transferring softened output distributions, matching intermediate representations, using multiple teachers or self-generated targets, and integrating compression with architecture search or pre-training. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact, practical models for deployment, but also reveals optimization and data-dependence limitations that motivate method refinements like task-adaptive search, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to transfer performance from large, expensive models to smaller, faster ones. The literature spans soft-label distillation from ensembles, feature- and representation-based matching, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, task-adaptive compression for large pretrained language models, and methods to transfer non-standard properties such as adversarial robustness. Empirical results demonstrate that properly designed distillation procedures can retain much of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, that internal-representation matching often improves downstream generalization beyond logits-only approaches, and that KD variants can be adapted to constraints such as limited (or private) data, distributed training, and resource- or latency-aware deployment. Open challenges include understanding which aspects of teacher knowledge are most useful for which student architectures and tasks, designing distillation under strict privacy or data-availability constraints, and transferring robustness properties reliably.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a flexible paradigm that improves efficiency, robustness, privacy, and generalization across modalities and tasks. KD can compress large pretrained models into lightweight deployable models, transfer internal representations to preserve teacher behaviors, operate without original training data, and be adapted to distributed and privacy-sensitive settings. Recent methodological advances—layer- and attention-aware projection, multi-teacher schedules, meta-learned teachers, and techniques connecting KD to regularization—make distillation a practical and theoretically grounded tool for both research and production NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deploying high-performing deep models under resource constraints by transferring information from large teacher models into smaller students. Approaches range from task-agnostic distillation and architecture search to layer-matching, internal representation imitation, data-free distillation, and techniques that adapt either the teacher or the student to improve transfer. Empirical work across vision and language shows these methods can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining much of the original performance, and task- or domain-aware strategies often yield the best practical trade-offs. Remaining challenges include robustness without access to original data, aligning heterogeneous inputs or modalities, and automating compression for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones across modalities (classification, sequence modeling, generation, graph-structured data, and federated systems). KD’s strengths arise not only from transferring teacher logits but also from transferring richer representation-level, adversarial, and self-derived signals. However, distillation has well-documented failure modes—optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, and domain or device heterogeneity—that require specific remedies. Combining representation-level objectives, teacher-friendly training, self-distillation or teacher-free approaches, and careful data strategies yields more robust and efficient compressed models while avoiding common pitfalls.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Adaptations, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large neural models in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models. Research has developed a spectrum of approaches — from matching logits to feature-level imitation, structural transformation of architectures, multi-teacher schemes, and task-specific adaptations — and has applied them across domains including detection, generative modeling, recommendation, retrieval, and multiple NLP tasks. Empirical work highlights both opportunities (substantial parameter reductions, faster inference, retained or modestly degraded accuracy) and pitfalls (propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, robustness concerns), motivating targeted algorithmic adjustments such as selective distillation, projector modules, and adversarially-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a flexible paradigm that improves efficiency, robustness, privacy, and generalization across modalities and tasks. KD can compress large pretrained models into lightweight deployable models, transfer internal representations to preserve teacher behaviors, operate without original training data, and be adapted to distributed and privacy-sensitive settings. Recent methodological advances—layer- and attention-aware projection, multi-teacher schedules, meta-learned teachers, and techniques connecting KD to regularization—make distillation a practical and theoretically grounded tool for both research and production NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, often ensemble or over-parameterized teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across computer vision, graph, generative, and language tasks, distillation reduces storage and inference cost while often retaining most of the teacher's accuracy. Methods range from matching output distributions to aligning intermediate representations or using adversarial generators when training data are unavailable. Distillation has been applied successfully to compress transformers and other large pretrained language models, to speed up question answering and reading-comprehension systems, and to produce compact models suitable for deployment on edge devices. At the same time, distillation faces challenges including loss of certain types of teacher knowledge, sensitivity to which samples are distilled, potential transfer or amplification of undesirable biases, and concerns about robustness and privacy. Recent work addresses these issues by selective sample weighting, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial data-free approaches, and robustness-aware objectives, suggesting a rich design space for future improvement.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Work across NLP and broader deep learning has developed multiple KD paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate-representation matching, layer-to-layer and many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher aggregation, and data-free distillation—and combined KD with other compression methods such as quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical results show that well-designed distillation can yield compact models that approach the accuracy of large pre-trained models while offering substantial savings in parameters, latency, and computational cost. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, coping with limited or unavailable training data, and selecting or weighting multiple teachers per example. The literature suggests principled strategies—attention-based layer fusion, representation-level losses, teacher confidence or dynamic weighting, and synthetic-data generation—that mitigate these issues and enable effective deployment of compressed models in domain-specific and resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been widely adopted to reduce model size and runtime while retaining performance. Work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows multiple complementary strategies—logit matching, feature mimicking, layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, and self-distillation—can be effective alone or in combination. Practical success depends on choices about teacher strength, student architecture, pre-training, and optimization, and recent systems integrate distillation with pruning, low-precision, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, a consistent set of practices has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate-layer matching, and task- or domain-specific adaptation—augmented by variants that address missing data, distributed training, privacy, and teacher-student mismatch. Empirical results show that distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while enjoying large gains in inference speed and memory, and recent work clarifies when and why distillation acts as an effective regularizer.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment. A diverse set of strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and intermediate representation matching to multi-teacher ensembles, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-supervised or privacy-preserving protocols—have been developed to preserve accuracy, robustness, and modality transfer while reducing inference cost. Practical systems combine distillation with quantization, pruning, or architecture search to meet application-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Methods, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or costly models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Research over the past decade shows multiple complementary mechanisms for effective distillation—soft-target supervision, feature and representation mimicking, layer-wise alignment, and task-aware selection of teacher knowledge. Practical advances adapt distillation to domain constraints (few-shot data, modality mismatch, federated or latency-constrained deployment) and model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph neural networks, generative models). Empirical work demonstrates that thoughtful choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features vs. relations), how to align layers, and how to prepare data and pretraining substantially affect student performance, sometimes enabling students to match or even surpass teachers under resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original logit-based teacher-student paradigm to include feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher strategies, and task- or hardware-aware compression. These methods have been applied across modalities — including vision, graphs, generative models, and a broad set of NLP tasks — and are increasingly combined with architecture search and pruning to meet deployment constraints. Despite empirical successes, important questions remain about what knowledge is most useful to transfer, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to operate under data, compute, or privacy limitations.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Tool for Compression, Adaptation, and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for transferring capabilities from large or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or modality-limited models. When combined with complementary strategies—domain adaptation, feature-level matching, data augmentation, and meta-learning—distillation enables practical deployment across constrained devices, heterogeneous federated systems, and domain-shifted settings. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization subtleties and mismatches between teacher and student require methodological care and, in some cases, alternative regularization strategies.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It is used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to protect privacy, and to adapt models across domains. Practical distillation methods vary in what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers are chosen (single, multi-teacher, self), and how training is regularized (data augmentation, loss design, adversarial objectives). While distillation often yields students that outperform similarly sized models trained from scratch, mismatches between teacher and student, optimization difficulties, and domain/privacy constraints remain important concerns. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful design choices (data augmentation, multi-stage distillation, private/noisy queries, and specialized losses) meaningfully affect student performance and deployment trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression techniques compress or replace large pretrained models with smaller, efficient models while aiming to retain much of the original performance. Modern work spans logit-based soft-label distillation, feature- and attention-based representation matching, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, online and mutual distillation schemes, meta-learned teachers, and approaches for resource- or data-constrained scenarios (including data-free and few-shot settings). Applications include compressing large language models into lightweight architectures for deployment, accelerating visual and multimodal models, enabling distributed training, and improving robustness and transfer. Key challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align heterogeneous architectures, preventing capacity mismatch and overfitting, and preserving task-relevant information while removing redundant representations. Empirical strategies that combine representation-level losses, task-aware selection, and online or meta-learning mechanisms tend to yield the best tradeoffs between efficiency and retained accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Roles, Limits, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly framed as a route to compress large models into smaller deployable students, but its benefits and pitfalls extend well beyond mere parameter reduction. KD acts as a form of learned regularization, can be applied in self-distillation and teacher-free regimes, and enables transferring properties such as robustness, privacy-preserving signals, and task-specific intermediate knowledge. At the same time, KD faces optimization and representation-mismatch challenges and can propagate undesirable biases from teacher to student. This paper argues that practitioners should treat KD as a flexible toolbox: combine soft-label supervision with internal-representation matching, flexible layer-mapping, attention-guided feature alignment, and targeted interventions for fairness, privacy, and robustness to get consistent benefits in both vision and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies enable deployment of large pretrained models by transferring function or representation from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) ones. Across supervised, self-supervised, and data-free settings, KD methods exploit soft targets, intermediate representation matching, architectural surgery, and data or training-time modifications to improve student accuracy, robustness, or efficiency. Empirical results show that appropriately designed distillation can retain most teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in model size, precision, or inference cost; but effectiveness depends on choices of targets, data, and teacher-student compatibility. Open challenges include preserving rare-token behavior in distilled NLP models, mitigating bias transfer, and jointly optimizing hardware constraints and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of practical and theoretical approaches for shrinking deep models while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, layer- and feature-level matching, architecture-aware transformations, teacher improvement or selection strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving pipelines, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-transfer applications, recent work shows that careful design choices—such as how layers are matched, which features to transfer, whether the teacher is static or trained to teach, and how to handle limited or private data—substantially affect the student’s final accuracy and deployment efficiency.
