papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while attempting to retain performance. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD variants address constraints such as limited computation, on-device heterogeneity, lack of access to teacher training data, fairness concerns, and the need for task-specific efficiency. Common themes include transferring softened output distributions, matching intermediate representations, using multiple teachers or self-generated targets, and integrating compression with architecture search or pre-training. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact, practical models for deployment, but also reveals optimization and data-dependence limitations that motivate method refinements like task-adaptive search, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression methods form a diverse toolkit for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of the performance of larger teachers. Research spans soft-label and self-distillation strategies, layer- and representation-level transfers, architecture-aware and task-adaptive compression, and deployment-aware approaches that combine pruning, quantization, and distillation. Empirical work shows that careful choice of distillation signal (logits, intermediate representations, or feature maps), alignment strategy between teacher and student layers, data augmentation, and optimization scheduling materially affects student performance. Practical systems exploit these design choices to compress large pre-trained language models, accelerate inference, enable heterogeneous-device training, or improve low-precision networks. Despite progress, open questions remain about principled objective design, sample efficiency under limited data, and theory connecting transferred representations to generalization.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Settings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models or ensembles to smaller “student” models. Work in this area spans methods that match final outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure; approaches that adapt teacher signals through meta-learning or task-aware filters; and specializations for settings such as vision–language, graph learning, federated or distributed training, and data-free scenarios. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but practical success depends on handling domain shift, architectural mismatch, heterogeneous data and devices, and the quality or calibration of teacher outputs. Important theoretical and statistical analyses have begun to clarify when and why distillation helps, but open problems remain around robust, privacy-preserving, and architecture-agnostic distillation for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Practical Prescriptions for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students suitable for deployment. While KD reliably reduces model size and inference cost, its effectiveness depends critically on choices around teacher design, the training signal (soft labels vs. representations), the data used for distillation, and additional constraints such as fairness and privacy. To realize reliable, high-quality compressed models in NLP and related domains, practitioners should treat KD as a system composed of complementary ingredients—data augmentation, multi-teacher or meta-learned teachers, representation-level objectives, and interventions for bias and privacy—rather than a single off-the-shelf loss.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning: Necessity, Challenges, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models and transferring desirable properties (accuracy, robustness, or representations) into smaller, deployable students. In NLP and related deep-learning domains, distillation enables the efficient use of pretrained teachers, supports domain adaptation and continual learning, and can be adapted for supervised, self-supervised, and adversarial objectives. However, naive distillation can degrade specific behaviors (e.g., lexical choices or uncertainty calibration) unless the distillation pipeline addresses alignment of inputs and representations, intermediate-layer supervision, the sample-wise effects of soft labels, and robustness transfer. I argue that distillation should be treated as a design problem—choosing which knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student representations, and when to expose students to raw or adversarial signals—to yield compact models that preserve both accuracy and desirable inductive properties.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies aim to transfer predictive behavior from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or more resource-efficient ones. The literature shows a variety of mechanisms (soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial feature matching), data- and training-focused interventions (data selection, augmentation, mixup, control of dataset complexity), and hybrid combinations with pruning or ensembling. Empirical results across NLP and vision tasks indicate that KD can preserve much of teacher performance while accelerating inference, but success depends strongly on (a) the choice of distillation targets and layer mappings, (b) the complexity and provenance of the distillation data, and (c) complementary techniques such as pre-training, feature-level matching, or structured pruning. Practical approaches therefore tailor the distillation recipe to model capacity, task characteristics, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Adaptations, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large neural models in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models. Research has developed a spectrum of approaches — from matching logits to feature-level imitation, structural transformation of architectures, multi-teacher schemes, and task-specific adaptations — and has applied them across domains including detection, generative modeling, recommendation, retrieval, and multiple NLP tasks. Empirical work highlights both opportunities (substantial parameter reductions, faster inference, retained or modestly degraded accuracy) and pitfalls (propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, robustness concerns), motivating targeted algorithmic adjustments such as selective distillation, projector modules, and adversarially-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It is used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to protect privacy, and to adapt models across domains. Practical distillation methods vary in what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers are chosen (single, multi-teacher, self), and how training is regularized (data augmentation, loss design, adversarial objectives). While distillation often yields students that outperform similarly sized models trained from scratch, mismatches between teacher and student, optimization difficulties, and domain/privacy constraints remain important concerns. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful design choices (data augmentation, multi-stage distillation, private/noisy queries, and specialized losses) meaningfully affect student performance and deployment trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision models while retaining much of their performance. Approaches range from matching teacher soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations and using contrastive or projection-based objectives. Practical training choices—such as which layers or features to mimic, how to filter or weight training samples, the role of data augmentation, and whether compact models are pre-trained—strongly affect outcomes. KD has been applied across domains (vision, language, graphs), combined with quantization and low-precision deployment, and adapted for resource-heterogeneous and latency-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights that KD works both by transferring relational/representational knowledge and by providing regularizing soft targets; effective distillation designs balance these mechanisms and tailor the transfer to task and capacity constraints.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical, Private, and Robust Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often framed narrowly as a model-compression trick to shrink large neural networks. This paper argues KD should instead be viewed as a core engineering and scientific tool for practical deployment: it enables training with limited or private data, yields task- and domain-adaptive compact models, improves robustness and fairness, and transfers intermediate representations and attention patterns that standard supervised training cannot. We synthesize evidence from recent work to show how variants of KD—self-distillation, layer-wise projection, multi-teacher schemes, teacher annealing, and data-free distillation—address concrete deployment challenges in vision and NLP, and we derive practical recommendations for combining these techniques in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Roles, Limits, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly framed as a route to compress large models into smaller deployable students, but its benefits and pitfalls extend well beyond mere parameter reduction. KD acts as a form of learned regularization, can be applied in self-distillation and teacher-free regimes, and enables transferring properties such as robustness, privacy-preserving signals, and task-specific intermediate knowledge. At the same time, KD faces optimization and representation-mismatch challenges and can propagate undesirable biases from teacher to student. This paper argues that practitioners should treat KD as a flexible toolbox: combine soft-label supervision with internal-representation matching, flexible layer-mapping, attention-guided feature alignment, and targeted interventions for fairness, privacy, and robustness to get consistent benefits in both vision and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations. Across modalities and tasks, distillation methods vary by what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate features, attention, or structural knowledge), by whether they rely on original training data, and by how the teacher-student relationship is optimized. Practical goals include reducing inference cost, preserving accuracy under domain shift, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, and improving robustness or fairness. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen transfer targets, training curricula, and data strategies can recover much of the teacher performance in compact models, and that meta-level and task-adaptive approaches further improve transfer effectiveness. Key open concerns are how to best align heterogeneous inputs or architectures, how to retain desirable inductive biases (e.g., for domain-specific tasks), and how to ensure reliable student performance without access to teacher training data.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a set of techniques that transfer knowledge from larger, expensive models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students) so the students retain much of the teacher utility while fitting deployment constraints. Research has produced a variety of distillation paradigms: logit- and soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer-wise and channel-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, self-supervised distillation, multi-teacher ensembles and domain-aware adaptation. Empirical work shows that combining pre-training for compact architectures with distillation, using task-aware selection of teacher signals, and tailoring distillation to modality- or task-specific structure leads to stronger compressed models. Important open issues include distillation without access to original data, preserving fairness and privacy in compressed models, and closing the capacity gap between teacher and student without over-constraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and empirically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and deployment constraints, KD enables moving from research-stage, high-capacity architectures to resource-efficient models suitable for latency- and privacy-constrained production. Realizing KD's full potential requires attention to teacher quality, data and domain mismatches, and scalability; appropriate choices—representation-level objectives, multi-teacher signals, online protocols, and privacy-aware distillation—address these challenges and make KD a core tool for applied deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger or more informed models to smaller ones. Methods vary from soft-label supervision and layer mapping to data-free generation, adversarial sample selection, federated and privacy-preserving protocols, and task- or domain-aware adaptation. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, and generative modeling show that distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, but performance depends sensitively on what information is transferred, how samples are selected, and whether pretraining or task adaptation is used. Practical use favors hybrids that combine architectural search, selective or weighted distillation, and generation or rehearsal strategies when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques condense information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable ones. Across vision, speech, recommendation, generative models, and natural language processing, practitioners use a mix of logit-based soft-label supervision, feature imitation, data distillation, multi-teacher fusion, curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware search to trade accuracy for latency, memory, or interpretability. Empirical work shows distilled students can often approach teacher accuracy while enabling deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings; theoretical and empirical analyses attribute much of KD’s effectiveness to the regularizing properties of soft targets, while recent extensions explicitly address adversarial robustness, decision-boundary transfer, domain adaptation, continual learning, and task-specific constraints. Remaining challenges include preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors (e.g., low-frequency phenomena), designing teacher-free or data-free alternatives, and building principled curricula and multi-source transfers that maximize student utility in downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Across settings—domain adaptation, resource-constrained deployment, privacy-limited releases, sequence generation, and large-scale distributed training—distillation methods enable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and cost. By leveraging teacher signals (soft targets, feature representations, or ensembles), self-distillation, and data- or communication-efficient protocols, practitioners can tailor compression strategies to meet production constraints without wholesale redesign of model architectures.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Power and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and practical approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and—in many cases—more deployable models. When combined with complementary techniques (pre-training of compact architectures, pruning, low-precision numerics, or data-free synthesis), distillation can retain much of a teacher model's performance while meeting latency, memory, or privacy constraints. However, the success of distillation is conditional on choices about teacher-student design, access to data or surrogates, and optimization strategies; awareness of these factors yields the most reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling deployment under resource constraints. Research over the past decade has developed variants that target outputs (soft labels), internal representations (layer-wise and attention-based methods), data regimes (data-free or distilled training sets), and architecture search for task-aware compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the practical gains and fundamental limits of distillation, and points to best practices such as pre-training compact models, selecting or synthesizing appropriate training data, and aligning student capacity to distilled signal.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Settings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models or ensembles to smaller “student” models. Work in this area spans methods that match final outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure; approaches that adapt teacher signals through meta-learning or task-aware filters; and specializations for settings such as vision–language, graph learning, federated or distributed training, and data-free scenarios. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but practical success depends on handling domain shift, architectural mismatch, heterogeneous data and devices, and the quality or calibration of teacher outputs. Important theoretical and statistical analyses have begun to clarify when and why distillation helps, but open problems remain around robust, privacy-preserving, and architecture-agnostic distillation for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to obtain compact models that retain much of the performance of larger models. Beyond simple logits matching, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, task-adaptive compression, privacy-preserving model release, and synergizes with structural compression techniques to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints in real-world systems. This article argues that KD should be a central component of modern model-compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, both in practice and in research directions.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies have become central tools to deploy large deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature shows diverse KD objectives (soft-label matching, representation matching, relational/correlation losses), architectural strategies (layer-wise, task-adaptive, student-friendly teacher training), data approaches (data augmentation, distilled or synthesized surrogates, zero-shot), and multi-teacher or ensemble-to-single compression. Empirical work across vision, generative models, reinforcement learning, and language tasks (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation) reveals consistent trade-offs between compression, accuracy, and robustness, and highlights practical constraints such as data heterogeneity and teacher-student capacity mismatch. Below we synthesize methods, observed benefits, limitations, and practical recommendations grounded in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Methods, Limits, and Complementary Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy to compress large pre-trained deep models so they can be deployed in latency- and resource-constrained settings. KD variants—multi-teacher pipelines, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, self-distillation, and feature-level matching—enable small students to approach or match teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost. KD is most effective when combined with complementary approaches such as pruning and architecture search, and when adapted to domain or system constraints (e.g., federated or multi-device settings). However, KD is not a universal panacea: data heterogeneity, misaligned inputs between teacher and student, and inappropriate augmentation or feature transfer can limit gains, so careful design choices are required to realize practical compression.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher model. Across computer vision, language, graph, and healthcare applications, KD variants augment or replace naive logit matching with feature/hint matching, data augmentation, layer mapping strategies, and data-free or privacy-aware mechanisms. Practical work emphasizes task-adaptive compression, many-to-many layer alignment for pre-trained transformers, and the use of synthetic or mixed inputs to improve student generalization. At the same time, theoretical and empirical studies highlight limitations under data heterogeneity and imperfect teachers, motivating hybrid losses that mix soft and hard labels and methods that control privacy leakage during distillation.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Capabilities, Limitations, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and graph domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, speed up training at scale, and allow transfer of robustness or domain expertise when carefully designed. However, successful distillation depends on alignment of teacher and student inputs/representations, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention, or contrastive embeddings), and careful handling of privacy, robustness, and domain shift. Best practice combines representation-level matching, adaptive teacher strategies, confidence-aware multi-teacher fusion, and privacy- or robustness-aware objectives to meet practical constraints while maximizing student performance.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones across modalities (classification, sequence modeling, generation, graph-structured data, and federated systems). KD’s strengths arise not only from transferring teacher logits but also from transferring richer representation-level, adversarial, and self-derived signals. However, distillation has well-documented failure modes—optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, and domain or device heterogeneity—that require specific remedies. Combining representation-level objectives, teacher-friendly training, self-distillation or teacher-free approaches, and careful data strategies yields more robust and efficient compressed models while avoiding common pitfalls.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring behavioral or representational information from a teacher to a student. Across computer vision and NLP, distillation methods vary from matching output soft targets to aligning internal representations, performing self-distillation, and synthesizing or selecting data when original training examples are unavailable. Empirical work shows distillation can retain much of teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, improved generalization, and deployment under latency or memory constraints. However, effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, layers, features), the availability and complexity of training data, regularization (e.g., label smoothing and augmentation), and fairness or privacy constraints. Open challenges include understanding when students can outperform teachers, balancing bias mitigation and utility, and combining distillation with pruning or hardware-aware compression for edge deployment.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Necessity for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Beyond simple logit matching, modern distillation encompasses feature-level mimicry, teacher adaptation, task-adaptive compression, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and continual or online schemes to maintain performance over time or across domains. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate teacher signals, intermediate-target losses, and deployment-aware architecture search—KD enables real-world use of large pretrained models in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment. A diverse set of strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and intermediate representation matching to multi-teacher ensembles, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-supervised or privacy-preserving protocols—have been developed to preserve accuracy, robustness, and modality transfer while reducing inference cost. Practical systems combine distillation with quantization, pruning, or architecture search to meet application-specific constraints.
